grid.projection: South polar stereographic on a 1737.4 km sphere, true scale at the pole; 0° longitude points up, 90°E right (LOLA convention).

layers.label: Elevation (shaded relief)
layers.resolution: 240 m source, 480 m display, 960 m readout
layers.what: Height relative to a 1737.4 km sphere. Crater floors near the pole sit 3–5 km below the ridges that catch sunlight.

layers.label: Slope
layers.resolution: 240 m slope baseline, averaged to 960 m
layers.what: How steep the ground is, from the LOLA elevation model over 240 m. Landers and rovers need gentle ground: Wueller et al. 2026 used < 8° for the Artemis lander. 240 m averaging hides steeper metre-scale slopes.

layers.label: Ruggedness
layers.what: Spread (standard deviation) of the sixteen 240 m slopes inside each cell: broken, lumpy ground scores high, an even plain or a smooth uniform slope scores low. It is km-scale terrain, not a rock count.

layers.label: High ground
layers.what: Height above (orange) or below (blue) the surrounding ~30 km. Near the pole the Sun skims the horizon, so high ridges see it most often: a rough proxy for sunlight, not an illumination model.

layers.label: Rock abundance
layers.what: Fraction of the surface covered by rocks larger than about 1 m, from how slowly the ground cools at night (Bandfield et al. 2011).
layers.statusNote: This global Diviner product covers 60°S–60°N only (night-time retrievals restricted to low latitudes), so it has no data poleward of 75°S. Slope, ruggedness and Mini-RF radar stand in for it here.

layers.label: Regolith temperature anomaly
layers.what: Night-time temperature of the fine soil relative to a model: warm = younger, more compacted regolith; cold = fluffier soil.
layers.statusNote: This global Diviner product covers 60°S–60°N only (night-time retrievals restricted to low latitudes), so it has no data poleward of 75°S. Slope, ruggedness and Mini-RF radar stand in for it here.

layers.label: Max temperature
layers.resolution: 2,880,000 model triangles (0.5 km grid, two per cell) binned to 960 m
layers.what: Hottest the surface gets in a year. Below about 110 K, water ice can survive at the surface for billions of years.
layers.coverageNote: Model grid spans ±300 km around the pole (to about 80°S along 0°/90°/180°/270° and 76°S at the corners); 44 % of this map has PRP values.

layers.label: Average temperature
layers.resolution: 2,880,000 model triangles (0.5 km grid, two per cell) binned to 960 m
layers.what: Year-round average 2 cm below the surface. It tracks how much sunlight a spot gets on average: warm = sunlit ridge, very cold = permanent shadow.
layers.coverageNote: Model grid spans ±300 km around the pole (to about 80°S along 0°/90°/180°/270° and 76°S at the corners); 44 % of this map has PRP values.

layers.label: Ice stability depth
layers.resolution: 2,880,000 model triangles (0.5 km grid, two per cell) binned to 960 m (cell value = median of its triangles)
layers.what: How deep you would dig before buried water ice could survive for a billion years (sublimation < 1 kg/m² per Gyr). 0 = stable right at the surface; grey = deeper than 2.87 m, the model's limit. A thermal model of where ice COULD last, not a detection of ice.
layers.coverageNote: Model grid spans ±300 km around the pole (to about 80°S along 0°/90°/180°/270° and 76°S at the corners); 44 % of this map has PRP values.

sentinels.-999: documented: deeper than 2.8738 m (1,847,439 triangles, all with annual max >= 203 K); shown grey
sentinels.-1: undocumented: only on the 100,319 coldest triangles (annual max <= 101.3 K); treated as 0 m, stable at the surface

layers.label: Cold traps
layers.resolution: 2,880,000 model triangles (0.5 km grid, two per cell) binned to 960 m
layers.what: Share of the cell whose annual maximum stays below 110 K: places cold enough to trap water ice at the surface.
layers.coverageNote: Model grid spans ±300 km around the pole (to about 80°S along 0°/90°/180°/270° and 76°S at the corners); 44 % of this map has PRP values.

layers.label: Distance to cold trap
layers.what: Straight-line distance to the nearest cell containing cold-trap ground (annual max < 110 K).

layers.label: Distance to shallow ice
layers.what: Straight-line distance to the nearest cell where the model says ice could survive within 1 m of the surface.

layers.label: Radar CPR (Mini-RF)
layers.what: Circular polarisation ratio of S-band radar echoes. High values (> 1) mean ground rough at the decimetre scale (blocky rocks, fresh craters) OR possibly ice: radar alone cannot tell them apart.

layers.label: Hydrogen (LEND)

dataset.name: LRO LEND averaged polar map (LRO-L-LEND-4/5-RDR-V1.0, ALDS, 2011-12-11 to 2016-09-14)

layers.coverageShort: Covers 80°S to the pole; blank right at the pole
layers.resolution: 0.5° cells below 80°S, smoothed over 15 km (LEND's collimated footprint is ~10 km)
layers.what: How many fewer epithermal neutrons escape here than on average at 80-83°S. Hydrogen slows neutrons, so blue (fewer neutrons) means more hydrogen in the top metre, most likely water ice; brown means drier than average. The signal is only a few per cent, so every value comes with its uncertainty.
layers.coverageNote: LEND's averaged polar product covers 80°S to the pole; cells with an uncertainty above 1.2 % (mostly within ~1° of the pole, where LRO spent little time per cell) are left blank.

features.name: Shackleton crater
features.note: 21 km crater whose rim touches the pole; its floor is in permanent shadow (IAU/USGS gazetteer centre).
